The gusli is an East Slavic many-stringed plucked instrument of the zither family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 314.122-5. The folk type has 11 to 36 gut or metal strings tuned to the natural scale, the strings parallel to the soundboard; it comes in a helmet shape and a wing shape, the former resting on the knees with the left hand damping strings to make harmony and the right hand sweeping across them, the latter smaller and held like a guitar. The nineteenth-century keyboard type has an iron frame and one octave of piano-style chromatic keys. It was played by wandering minstrels, it appears in East Slavic epic, and it once supplied musicians to the court.
古斯里琴為多弦撥奏齊特琴，弦平行於共鳴板；民間型有十一至三十六弦，採自然音階調音: The gusli is a many-stringed plucked zither with the strings parallel to the soundboard; the folk type has eleven to thirty-six strings and is tuned to the natural scale. The helmet shape rests on the knees, the right hand sweeping the strings and the left damping them to make chords; the wing shape is smaller, closer to the Baltic zither, and the left hand damps through an opening in the body. Changes of volume and timbre come mainly from plucking, sweeping and damping, not from a bow or a striker. The nineteenth-century keyboard type adds an iron frame and one octave of chromatic keys; pressing a key lifts the dampers of the matching strings, so chords can be arpeggiated.
古斯里琴為東斯拉夫最古老的多弦撥弦樂器，根源在諾夫哥羅德共和國的大諾夫哥羅德。文: The gusli is the oldest many-stringed plucked instrument of the East Slavs, rooted in Novgorod the Great in the Novgorod Republic. Written mentions go back to 591, when the Greek historian Theophylact Simocatta described the Slavs using it, though the word in early use may have referred to string instruments in general; the earliest firm record is from Novgorod the Great in 1170. There are two forms: the helmet shape was widespread in the south and west of Kievan Rus, and the smaller wing shape is found in northern regions such as Novgorod and Pskov. The iron-framed keyboard gusli appeared in the nineteenth century, with one octave of chromatic keys. The Ukrainian husla was kept in use longer, and in the eighteenth century there was a playing school at Hlukhiv that supplied musicians to the Russian court.

The nineteenth-century keyboard gusli has an iron frame, stands on a support or on table legs, and has one octave of piano-style chromatic keys; pressing a key lifts the dampers of all the strings of that note. 古斯里琴的聆聽場合主要見於東斯拉夫民間與敘事傳統：流浪藝人斯科莫羅赫以它伴奏，古: The gusli is mostly heard in East Slavic folk and narrative tradition: the skomorokh wandering minstrels accompanied themselves on it, and the old East Slavic heroic epics describe it as an instrument beloved of warriors. In Ukraine the husla once accompanied elderly nobles, and in the nineteenth century it was mostly used by clergy; the Hlukhiv school also supplied players to the Russian court. The folk gusli is laid across the knees, the right hand plucking and the left damping to make chords; the nineteenth-century keyboard gusli controls the dampers with piano-style chromatic keys and can arpeggiate.
